summary: Defines a MIME content type for message disposition notifications, which report what happened to a message after delivery, plus header fields to request them. It is an Internet Standard.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 8098 defines Message Disposition Notifications (MDNs), which report what a mail program did with a delivered message. A recipient may ignore a request, and an MDN does not prove that anyone read or understood the message.

questions: what is a message disposition notification
how do email read receipts work
can a read receipt be ignored
subtitle: A machine-readable email report for what happened to a message after delivery.

tldr.problem: Mail senders need a standard way to request and receive information about a message's disposition after delivery, without overriding the recipient's privacy.
tldr.mechanism: A sender may include a Disposition-Notification-To header. If the recipient's mail user agent chooses to respond, it sends a multipart/report containing a machine-readable message/disposition-notification part.
tldr.outcome: An MDN can report that a message was displayed, dispatched, processed or deleted, but it is only a request-based report, not proof that the recipient read or understood the message. RFC 8098 obsoletes RFC 3798 and updates RFCs 2046 and 3461.

today: RFC 8098 is an Internet Standard (STD 85). It obsoletes RFC 3798 and updates RFC 2046 and RFC 3461.

sections.title: What an MDN Reports
sections.content:
A Message Disposition Notification (MDN) reports a message's disposition after successful delivery. The RFC's examples include displaying, printing, forwarding, processing or deleting a message, as well as a recipient refusing to send an MDN.

The format is intended for people and software. It can help a sender associate a notification with a message and recipient, including after forwarding, and it can carry notifications between Internet Mail and other mail systems through gateways.
sections.plainLanguage: An MDN reports an action taken by a mail program after delivery. It is designed so people can read it and software can process it.

sections.title: Requesting a Notification
sections.content:
A sender requests an MDN with a Disposition-Notification-To header containing one or more notification addresses. The recipient's user agent may ignore the request. The RFC strongly recommends asking for user consent and says the default should be not to send an MDN.

An MDN must not be sent automatically when the request address differs from Return-Path, when Return-Path is missing, or when multiple distinct notification addresses are present. The user must confirm, and if confirmation is not possible, no MDN is sent. A user agent must not send more than one MDN for each recipient, and an MDN must not request another MDN.

Original-Recipient can preserve the address as specified by the sender, while Disposition-Notification-Options provides an extension point. A Message-ID is especially useful for matching an MDN to its original message.
sections.plainLanguage: The header asks for a notification but does not force the recipient's mail program to send one. Consent rules reduce unwanted disclosure, mail loops and message floods.

sections.title: The Multipart MDN Format
sections.content:
An MDN is a MIME multipart/report message with report type disposition-notification. Its first part is a human-readable explanation. Its second part has media type message/disposition-notification and contains fields for software to process. An optional third part may return the original message or part of it.

The MDN is sent to the address in the original request. Its From field identifies the person for whom it is issued, and its transport envelope sender is null. It must not request an MDN itself, and its Message-ID, if present, must differ from the original message's ID. Each MDN describes one message for one recipient.

The machine-readable part uses 7bit encoding so that non-MIME mail readers can display it.
sections.plainLanguage: An MDN has a readable explanation and a separate part with fields for software. It may also include the original message, but it describes only one recipient's disposition.

sections.title: Fields That Describe the Disposition
sections.content:
The machine-readable part uses fields formatted like email headers. Final-Recipient and Disposition are required. Other fields may identify the reporting mail program, a gateway, the original recipient, the original message ID or an error. The Original-Recipient field is included only when the original address is reliably known.

The Disposition field combines how the action occurred with what happened. Its modes distinguish user-directed from automatic actions and manual from automatic sending. Its types are displayed, dispatched, processed and deleted. Displayed means the message was shown to someone, not that it was read or understood. New extension fields and modifiers use IANA registration rules.

Reporting-UA can help identify interoperability problems, but the RFC warns against unnecessary detail that could identify or fingerprint a user.
sections.plainLanguage: The report names the recipient and the action the mail program took. The word displayed means the message was shown, not that someone read it.

sections.title: Consent, Gateways and Conformance
sections.content:
A user agent or gateway conforms by generating MDNs according to the specification; it need not generate every possible disposition value. The original recipient may receive more than one MDN when an address is forwarded to multiple recipients. A mailing-list exploder may treat successful delivery to the list as the final disposition and avoid forwarding the request to every subscriber.

The RFC gives non-binding guidance for gateways that translate notifications from other mail systems. A gateway should preserve original-recipient and message-ID information when available, and an MDN translated from a foreign system must identify the gateway in its MDN-Gateway field. A request should not be gatewayed to a system without a separate notification address when that would send the response to the wrong address.
sections.plainLanguage: Gateways can translate notifications between mail systems, but should preserve the recipient and message identifiers when possible. Mailing lists can avoid sending a separate receipt request to every subscriber.

sections.title: Forgery, Privacy and Mail Bombing
sections.content:
MDNs can be forged like ordinary email, and a forged message can trick a recipient into sending an unsolicited notification. Mail software should process requests only after checking the message's authenticity. An MDN may reveal when a message was displayed, which mail program was used and details about the sender's environment. A recipient can ignore requests, and user agents should not send them automatically.

A notification cannot prove that a message was or was not seen: it may be lost, forged or bypassed. A false notification address can also direct a flood of MDNs to a third party. Since an MDN may include the original message, its size can exceed that of the triggering message and amplify traffic.
sections.plainLanguage: An MDN can be faked and can reveal information about when and how someone uses email. It is not proof that a message was read, and automatic replies can be abused to flood another mailbox.

items.label: Displayed
items.desc: Shown by the mail user agent; reading is not guaranteed.

items.label: Dispatched
items.desc: Sent elsewhere, for example printed, faxed or forwarded.

items.label: Processed
items.desc: Handled by a rule or server without being displayed.

items.label: Deleted
items.desc: Deleted; the recipient may or may not have seen it.
